explain.say: How do you study something far too small to see? With clever experiments, over more than a hundred years! Look at the timeline. It starts in 1803, when John Dalton in England said everything is made of tiny solid balls called atoms.

explain.say: In 1897, JJ Thomson found the electron, a tiny negative particle. So atoms were not solid balls after all! Look at 1904: his plum pudding model, with electrons dotted in a ball of positive charge, like raisins in a cake. Can you picture it?

faq.a: In 1803 John Dalton said all matter is made of tiny atoms that cannot be split, and that atoms of one element are all alike. He pictured them as solid balls.
asks: What did Dalton say about atoms?

faq.q: What was the plum pudding model?
faq.a: JJ Thomson's 1904 model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons dotted through it, like raisins in a pudding.
asks: Who made the plum pudding model?

faq.q: What did the gold foil experiment show?
faq.a: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold, so atoms are mostly empty space. A few bounced back, so there must be a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

faq.q: Why did the model of the atom keep changing?
faq.a: Each new experiment found evidence the old model could not explain, so scientists improved the model. That is how science works.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. It explained why atoms are heavier than their protons alone.

facts: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
Rutherford proposed the nuclear model of the atom in 1911, after the Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment of 1909.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

quiz.say: Why did a few alpha particles bounce back from the gold foil?
quiz.show: Why did a few alpha particles bounce back from the gold foil?

options.show: They hit a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
options.say: They hit a tiny, dense, positive nucleus

quiz.why: Only a small, heavy, positive centre could push them straight back.

wrong.1: Electrons are far too light to bounce alpha particles back.
wrong.2: The foil was extremely thin; most particles went straight through.

quiz.why: Dalton's idea was in 1803, long before Bohr in 1913 and Chadwick in 1932.

wrong.1: The neutron was found in 1932, the last of these.
